description_full: Genco Shipping & Trading Limited, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the ocean transportation of drybulk cargoes worldwide. It operates through two segments: major bulk and minor bulk fleet. The company owns and operates dry bulk vessels to transports iron ore, grains, coal, steel products, and other drybulk cargoes. It charters its vessels primarily to trading houses, including commodities traders; producers; and government-owned entities. Genco Shipping & Trading Limited was incorporated in 2004 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: Genco Shipping & Trading Limite is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.1B market cap on $342M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -14% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are contracting by -3.4pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The business throws off $29M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 0.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 16% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 74% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 9% below the high.

The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 50%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $5.64 to $13.09 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.5% (vs the 8% bar).

The price implies 14.4% annual cash-flow growth, 16pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 20.35).

Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 2/9.

hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.6x net debt to EBITDA ($55.5M of cash against $189.1M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 0.6x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -14.0% over 3 years, -0.8% over 5 years and 8.3% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 34%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -2.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (0.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 15.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 60%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (23 sales, net $60.5M sold).
It returns 2.9% a year to shareholders (6.9% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.8% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 1,056 employees, each generates about $324K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median.
That works out to $27K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (6x revenue per employee).
